assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a rare case where a clean continuum model (the Bistritzer-MacDonald band theory predicting flat bands at a magic angle) was followed by experiment showing correlated insulators and superconductivity. It opened moire quantum matter as a tunable platform for correlated electrons. I value that the mechanism is simple, general and analyzable, and that theory and experiment are tightly linked.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the decisive prediction in 2011; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the 2018 experimental discovery of correlated and superconducting states. This theory-plus-experiment trio is a fair and compact configuration. Whether other experimental groups or the original twistronics ideas also deserve credit is not settled by the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Strongly replicated by many independent groups over about eight years, with a large follow-on literature (fractional Chern insulators, other moire systems). Timely for recognition, though the origin of the superconductivity is still debated.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene is unresolved.
Credit for early twist-angle ideas and the experimental precursors (including those not in the credited names) may be contested.
I rely on my own recollection of the literature, not independent verification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kane and Mele's Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators identified a new topological phase of matter, protected by symmetry, and launched the field of topological insulators. The idea is conceptually clean and universal, and the experimental realization in HgTe wells gave it a concrete test. Its impact on condensed-matter theory and materials is lasting.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical founding contribution; Molenkamp's group provided the quantum spin Hall experiment in HgTe following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. The omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and of the 3D topological insulator work by Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan, makes the configuration incomplete. Haldane, Thouless and Kosterlitz were already recognized in 2016 for topological phases.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed experimentally and widely extended (3D insulators, photonic and cold-atom analogs), with a stable interpretation. Recognition is timely, but the overlap with the 2016 prize is a consideration.
uncertainties: Credit is divided among several theory groups, including some not in the supplied names.
The degree to which the 2016 prize already covers the conceptual core.
Practical applications remain limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realize Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters and have become a quantum simulator for many-body physics, including the Mott insulator transition. Seeing textbook statistical-mechanics models realized in a clean experiment fits my preference for model systems that can be controlled and analyzed.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch-Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard realization; Greiner, Bloch and Hansch observed the superfluid-Mott transition; Esslinger's group realized Fermi-Hubbard physics. The field has many contributors, and the five-name credit exceeds three, so a choice is unavoidable. I choose a theory-experiment mix, but the experimental side (Greiner or Esslinger versus Bloch) is open.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with extensive independent confirmation and a rich subsequent literature, though the quantum simulation of truly hard problems is still developing. Cirac and Zoller also appear under a separate quantum-computation candidate, which could overlap.
uncertainties: Allocation among five credited names is unclear, and the choice of Bloch over Greiner or Esslinger is debatable.
Possible overlap with the Cirac-Zoller quantum-computation entry.
The practical value of quantum simulation beyond classical computation is not yet fully proven.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theory of crackling noise and depinning describes universal avalanche statistics in disordered systems (Barkhausen noise, earthquakes, plasticity) through the renormalization group. It is a prime example of finding universal results behind messy systems, which I regard as physics at its best.
assessment.attribution: Fisher's functional RG for depinning and charge-density waves was foundational; Sethna, Dahmen and collaborators developed the universal scaling and experimental connections for Barkhausen noise. The credit is reasonably clean for a trio, though the relative role of Fisher versus Sethna-Dahmen should be examined.
assessment.maturity: The theory is mature and has been tested in magnets, plasticity and other systems, but the quantitative agreement with experiment varies and some claims of universality are debated.
uncertainties: Experimental verification of universality classes is uneven across systems.
How broadly the theory should be credited versus earlier depinning and RG work.
Public impact beyond the community is modest.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Geometric and topological phases in quantum mechanics are conceptually deep. The Aharonov-Bohm effect showed that potentials have physical consequences, and Berry's phase underlies much of modern band topology, molecular physics and optics. The understanding is central and general.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) are the original source; David Bohm is deceased, which constrains the configuration, and Ehrenberg and Siday anticipated the effect. Berry's 1984 phase is a distinct and decisive contribution (with Pancharatnam and Longuet-Higgins as precursors). Pairing the two is reasonable, but the credit history is intricate.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed for decades and enormously influential, so this is not premature; if anything it is late, which raises the question of whether the discovery is best recognized now.
uncertainties: Bohm cannot be a laureate, and the credit of Ehrenberg and Siday and of Pancharatnam is unresolved.
Two distinct discoveries separated by 25 years are combined in one candidate, and each may need separate recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The jamming transition proposes a unified, critical-like picture of rigidity onset in disordered matter (foams, grains, glasses). It is a simple geometric mechanism with universal scaling that connects soft matter and statistical physics. This resonates with my interest in clean models of complex materials.
assessment.attribution: Liu and Nagel introduced the jamming phase diagram and developed the picture with O'Hern, Silbert and Witten; the two-person credit is plausible but the contribution of others, including Torquato and Parisi's work on hard-sphere and mean-field jamming, is substantial and unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by simulation and several experiments, yet the relation to the glass transition and the universality classes remain actively debated, so the interpretation is not fully stable.
uncertainties: The theoretical status of jamming versus the glass transition is not settled.
Credit overlap with mean-field theory of hard spheres and with other groups.
Experimental tests rely heavily on simulation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube opened high-energy neutrino astronomy by detecting a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux and associating neutrinos with a blazar (TXS 0506+056) and the Galactic plane. A new observational window of this kind is a large achievement in instrument-driven physics.
assessment.attribution: Halzen led the IceCube concept and scientific program; Spiering was a key early leader of the Baikal and AMANDA/IceCube efforts. The large collaboration makes any two-person credit an inevitable simplification, and the Baikal and AMANDA pioneers (and others such as Learned and Markov) are also relevant.
assessment.maturity: Detections of the diffuse flux are statistically solid, but the source identification is still developing, so the astrophysical interpretation is still maturing.
uncertainties: Specific source associations remain at modest significance.
Large-collaboration credit is hard to allocate fairly.
Outside my own field, so I have limited ability to judge instrument details.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Intermittency and multifractal scaling in fully developed turbulence are core questions in statistical physics, with Kolmogorov 1941 theory corrected by anomalous scaling. From my own work on turbulent transport I know the importance of this problem, but I also recognize that no first-principles derivation of anomalous exponents exists.
assessment.attribution: Frisch (with Parisi, Sulem) developed the multifractal model and the Kolmogorov-based theory; Sreenivasan led the experimental measurement of scaling. Kolmogorov, Kraichnan, Parisi and others made foundational contributions, so the credit for the decisive step is unclear.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally and numerically well supported, but the mechanism is not understood from first principles, which makes recognition arguably premature for a prize that rewards a resolved discovery.
uncertainties: Lack of a derivation of anomalous exponents.
Prior contributors (Kolmogorov, Kraichnan, Parisi) complicate attribution.
My own field means I must be careful about possible bias.
